name: Felix Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Felix. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to any company, union or government, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. Could you start by telling me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt for a living. I drive a dozer, a bulldozer, at the open-cut coal mine at Hollins Vale, mostly on the dumps where the waste rock goes, shaping it so it doesn't slide.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that look like across a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Start at seven, check the tracks and the blade, then I'm on the dump all day, pushing, levelling, cutting the edges back so the trucks can tip safely. It's not glamorous, but you can see what you've done at the end, a nice flat pad or a clean batter, which is the slope. I eat lunch in the cab most days, radio on, nobody bothering me. That's the bit I'd miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing, to be honest. I'm not online much and I don't talk about this stuff at the tea break. If somebody asked, I'd say, there you go, another thing that didn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan holds. I'm aiming to finish at sixty-two, four years from now, and the mine's got about twelve years of coal left anyway. The coal running out worries me more than computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. I'd turn up, push dirt, pay the bills and put a bit aside. Annika's salon does fine, so between us we're okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Normal. Nothing to feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use any of this stuff. What does AI look like at your mine right now, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a remote dozer they try now and then on the far dump, run from a trailer by a young fella with two joysticks. It's slow and it gets stuck. I've never touched a chatbot and I don't plan to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said coal running out worries you more. Can you tell me about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every few years there's talk the mine closes early because of the price or the government. My brother lost his job at a smaller pit up the road in 2019. That's the real danger round here, not robots.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, another thing that didn't happen, if anyone asked. I'm not online much and I don't talk about this stuff at the tea break.
S0.think: Privately it means my plan to finish at sixty-two holds. The mine's coal running out worries me more than computers do.
S0.do: Carries on pushing dirt, paying bills and putting a bit aside each month. Relies on his wife's salon income alongside his own as before.
S0.feel: Fine and normal, with nothing much to feel.
S0.quote: There's a remote dozer they try now and then on the far dump, run from a trailer by a young fella with two joysticks.
S0.fieldNote: Felix is completely calm here and steers the talk to coal running out, which is his long-standing worry. He describes the remote dozer trial with mild scorn. He doesn't use AI and has no plans to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, they'll do what makes money, always have. I wouldn't get on any soapbox about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a dozer on a dump is a fairly simple job to hand to a machine, simpler than people think. If the remote dozer gets good, they won't need three of us per shift. I'm not the best operator, I'm not the worst, so it'd come down to luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and wait to see who they pick. I'd put a bit more away, maybe two hundred extra a month, and pay off the last of the boat loan. I wouldn't do any training unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it'd be there when I'm sitting in the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they asked you to train on the remote dozer, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made it a condition, I'd do it, grumbling. But I'd be hopeless with the joysticks and a screen. I'd rather they offered me a package and let me go a year early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Annika say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd tell me to stop moping and go fishing more. She's the practical one. She'd also say the salon's not going anywhere, robots can't do a perm, and she's probably right.

S1.say: I'd say it's business and companies will do what makes money, as they always have. I wouldn't get on any soapbox about it.
S1.think: Privately I think a dozer on a dump is a simple job to hand to a machine. If they cut from three operators a shift, it would come down to luck for an average operator like me.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and waits to see who is picked for cuts. Saves about two hundred extra a month and clears the boat loan, avoiding training unless it's required.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not losing sleep, with the worry sitting with him in the cab.
S1.quote: She'd also say the salon's not going anywhere, robots can't do a perm, and she's probably right.
S1.fieldNote: Felix's centrist shrug, 'it's business', covers a private recognition that dozing a waste dump is easy to automate. He'd rather take a package than learn to run a remote unit. His wife's steady salon income gives him quiet comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it's mad and nobody saw it coming, which would be true. I still wouldn't post anything, but I'd be talking about it at the pub like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty with no job, and nobody's hiring a sixty-year-old dozer driver when the dozers drive themselves. We've got about three months put by. Annika's salon would carry the basics, but only the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sell the boat, no question, and we'd stop eating out. I'd take whatever redundancy they offered rather than fight it. After, I'd try to pick up farm work round Hollins Vale, cleaning out dams and clearing fence lines on hired gear, for as long as farmers still pay a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Bit numb, like I'd just been told it rather than imagining it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years' warning compare with a slower version, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. I'd be four years short of my plan, and there's no time to save the difference. With more time I could at least sit tight and let the clock run out on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do farm work on hired gear. Is that something you've done before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bits and pieces, for my brother-in-law on weekends. A farmer pays cash and doesn't ask for a certificate. Mind you, if the robots can push a dump, they can clean a dam too, so I'm not kidding myself it'd last.

S2.say: I'd say it's mad and nobody saw it coming. I wouldn't post anything, but I'd be talking about it at the pub like everyone else.
S2.think: Privately I'd be sixty with no job and nobody hiring a dozer driver when the dozers drive themselves. With about three months saved, my wife's salon would cover only the basics.
S2.do: Sells the boat and stops eating out straight away, and takes whatever redundancy is offered. Afterwards picks up cash farm work clearing dams and fence lines on hired machines for as long as farmers still pay a person.
S2.quote: If the robots can push a dump, they can clean a dam too, so I'm not kidding myself it'd last.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year version cuts four years off Felix's plan, and he feels it as a blunt loss. He doesn't blame anyone; he just reaches for cash farm work he already knows. He is clear-eyed that this fallback would also be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, it's business. Maybe I'd add that they should look after the older workers with a decent package.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three, past my sixty-two. So really, if the mine keeps me to the end of my plan, I'm out before it lands. The worry is whether they start cutting dozer crews in year two or three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, put the boat up for sale when the price is right rather than in a hurry, and tell the supervisor I'd take an early package if there was one at sixty-one. I'd keep away from training as long as they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. It's like watching the weather from the cab, you can see it coming over the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay away from training. If a younger operator got trained and you didn't, how would that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be annoyed, I won't pretend. But I've made my bed. I'm not going to be a fifty-nine-year-old learner on joysticks to save two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kirsten's in the army, she'll be fine, they'll always need people for something. Sasha's got the two little ones, and her husband drives trucks. I'd tell him to start looking now, more than I'd worry about myself.

S3.say: I'd say it's business, as before, and maybe add that companies should look after older workers with a decent package.
S3.think: Privately five years takes me to sixty-three, past my planned finish at sixty-two. The worry is whether dozer crews get cut in year two or three before I'm out.
S3.do: Saves harder and sells the boat when the price is right rather than in a rush. Tells his supervisor he'd take an early package at sixty-one and avoids training as long as possible.
S3.feel: A bit anxious, like seeing weather come over the hill from the cab.
S3.quote: I'm not going to be a fifty-nine-year-old learner on joysticks to save two years.
S3.fieldNote: Five years nearly covers Felix to his planned finish, but he worries about cuts landing early. He chooses not to retrain and owns the cost of that openly. His concern moves quickly to his son-in-law, a truck driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and who knows. Plenty of things are meant to be ten years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be gone by then. I'd be sixty-eight, fishing off the jetty at Long Bay. The coal mine might be shut by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd work to sixty-two, keep saving, keep the boat. I'd maybe mention to my son-in-law that trucking might not be a forever job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's somebody else's problem, and I don't mean that unkindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'somebody else's problem'. Whose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones, and the governments. I've got nothing against them doing something, as long as it's sensible and not just handing money out. I just won't be the one standing in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year version that could still go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine shut early for other reasons, I'd be in trouble either way. And if the robots got cheap fast and they didn't wait the ten years. But I can't plan for every if.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and who knows. Plenty of things are supposed to be ten years away.
S4.think: Privately I'd be gone by then, sixty-eight and fishing off the jetty. The coal mine might be shut anyway by then.
S4.do: Works to sixty-two as planned, keeps saving and keeps the boat. May warn his son-in-law that trucking might not be a lifelong job.
S4.feel: Calm, seeing it as someone else's problem without meaning it unkindly.
S4.quote: I'd be sixty-eight, fishing off the jetty at Long Bay.
S4.fieldNote: Felix is calm in the ten-year version because his age simply puts him beyond it. He supports sensible government action but is wary of handouts, a typical centre stance. His remaining worry is a mine closure for other reasons.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd lose four years I've counted on. A decent redundancy package and being allowed to draw my pension a bit early without being stung for it. That'd do me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people round here have lived with the mine maybe closing for twenty years. We're used to bad news. Robots are just a new kind of it.

headlineQuote: We're used to bad news. Robots are just a new kind of it.
portrait: Felix Jensen is a 58-year-old dozer operator on the waste dumps of an open-cut coal mine at Hollins Vale, a man who likes eating lunch alone in his cab and has never touched a chatbot. He sees companies' choices as just business and worries more about coal running out than about computers. He is calm under the plateau, uneasy under steady change, alarmed if AGI comes in two years and costs him four years he's counted on, and anxious with five. With ten years he expects to be fishing and calls it somebody else's problem, though he worries for his son-in-law, a truck driver.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take away four years of work he has been counting on before retiring at sixty-two.
whatWouldHelp: A decent redundancy package and being allowed to draw his pension a bit early without a penalty.
